title: More Pentests Without More Pentesters: Where AI Safely Helps
content_md: Demand for penetration testing keeps rising, be it due to DORA threat-led testing, NIS2, or customer security questionnaires. However, supply often cannot keep up. Experienced testers are scarce, take months to hire and train, and every one of them spends part of each engagement on work that is not testing. For a company that sells hours, that unbillable part is the margin. This article shows how to measure it, which parts AI can take over, and how to do that without sending client vulnerabilities to someone else's servers. Most companies track billable testing time and lack a number for the rest. If you tag the last ten engagements by phase, the picture usually changes: Writing findings, screenshots, formatting Report handover, status questions, retest Two ratios matter: documentation plus review as a share of testing time, and calendar days from last testing day to report delivery. The first sums up to the hidden cost, but only the second is what clients feel. The tasks that suit a language model are the ones where the tester already knows the answer and needs it written down: It will be helpful to decide beforehand in what capacity to keep humans on severity decisions, exploit validation and anything the client will rely on as a statement of fact. A model that confidently describes and is set to run an exploit chain that nobody verified can be is worse than no help.
